author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Six Tables and One Teapot
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
The trouble with the Six Tables feast was that there were only five usable tables.

The sixth had a loose leg.

Mara discovered the problem while placing bread on it. One basket leaned. The other followed. She caught both, but not before declaring the furniture an insult to bakers everywhere.

"I made that table," Tamsin said.

"Then you know who to complain to."

Iroh set down his teapot.

"Perhaps we could put it near the wall and reserve it for cups."

Mara pointed at the wobble.

"Do you want the tea in the cups or on the floor?"

I rubbed the bridge of my nose.

The feast was supposed to be simple. A community meal on Lanternwell Square, free to attend, with food brought by anyone who wished and enough seating for people who needed it. Greg had agreed to play music. Katara had arranged for two clinic volunteers to help serve. Neri had promised not to count how many guests arrived because the new privacy protocol made that an increasingly unpopular habit.

Iroh drew six rectangles in a dusting of spilled flour. "If the serving pots stand here, the queue blocks the clear route. We must move them."
"Onto the cables?" Greg called from his amplifier. "Because I'm pretty sure the electrician has feelings about that."
Iroh shifted the imaginary pots. "A sound objection. You understand your battlefield."
"Mostly I understand extension cords. Lost a gig to one once."
Tamsin arrived with a measuring tape. She marked an actual safe aisle and told them both to move their equipment until the route was clear, not merely clear from where they stood.
Mina counted bowls. Mara counted loaves. Nobody had enough volunteers to wash everything afterward.
"Then six tables present a seventh problem," Iroh said.
"That's not a strategy," Mara told him. "That's dishes."
He rolled up his sleeves and carried two baskets without defending himself. Greg followed with a coil of cable, humming a tune that sounded suspiciously like a sound check performed backward.
Later I watched them from the service line. Iroh thought in routes, ingredients, and people who had to be asked rather than commanded. Greg thought in rhythms, borrowed equipment, and getting a laugh when a microphone refused to cooperate. They were both kind. They were absolutely not the same man.

Then everyone arrived at once.

Aang came through the Riverstone Door carrying three boxes of flatbread. Toph followed, announcing that the floor near the eastern arch was "one good sneeze from embarrassment." Danse appeared with tools because somebody had mentioned a table. Greg brought two folding chairs and a guitar.

Maui brought a banner.

The banner read SIX TABLES, ONE HEART.

I stared at it.

"Maui."

"What?"

"One heart?"

"It's a metaphor."

"It's a terrible metaphor."

He looked wounded. "It's festive."

"Some of us would like more than one heart involved in a community dinner."

He glanced toward Iroh, then at Greg, and finally understood why I was trying so hard not to laugh.

"Fine," he said. "Six tables. Many hearts."

"Better."

He went to find fresh paint.

Iroh watched the exchange over the rim of his cup.

"Your patience is being tested."

"My patience left at breakfast."

"Then we will have to make tea without it."

He had agreed to serve one modest pot of the better leaves for the feast, while the pantry volunteers handled the larger kettles. It was a good plan. We had even written it down.

Then a guest arrived carrying a jug of milk and asked whether anyone had considered a child with a dairy allergy.

Katara was already checking the labels.

Greg set his guitar aside and helped move the milk to a separate table. Toph tapped a foot against the stone and announced that the sixth table was not the only thing wobbling.

By noon, the square had become a collection of small problems, none catastrophic, all capable of making someone feel unwelcome.

I found Pip near the fountain with a stack of place cards.

"Why are there names on the chairs?" I asked.

"People thought it would be easier to seat everyone by the person they came with."

I picked up a card bearing my name and saw three more cards beside it.

My stomach sank.

"Who wrote these?"

"Someone from the welcome committee."

"Did they ask any of us?"

Pip shook their head.

I put the cards back in the stack.

"Then we won't use them."

It would have been easy to laugh. People were fascinated by who sat next to whom, as though a dinner arrangement could explain all the choices that made a relationship honest. But I had promised the people I cared about that our private agreements wouldn't become decorations for a public event.

We removed the cards.

A few people complained. Iroh explained that the tables belonged to everyone, not to whichever gossip had reached the square first.

"Guests may sit wherever they are comfortable," he said. "Or stand. Or eat at home. Hospitality is not an examination."

I wanted to kiss him for that. Instead, I carried a tray.

The feast began late.

Greg played a song about repairing chairs that made Tamsin threaten to throw a hammer into the canal. Katara directed the clinic volunteers with the focused patience of someone who had triaged considerably worse situations. Aang talked with two children about the difference between games and traditions that deserved context.

Maui returned with a corrected banner.

SIX TABLES, MANY HEARTS, PLEASE DO NOT SIT ON THE BROKEN ONE.

It was perfect.

I almost told him so.

Then I noticed the guest at the far edge of the square.

They were sitting on a low wall with an untouched bowl, their shoulders hunched. People passed in front of them without looking directly at their face. It was possible they wanted to be left alone. It was also possible they had nowhere to sit.

I took a spare chair from the stack and stopped a few feet away.

"Would you like a chair?" I asked.

"No, thank you."

"All right."

I turned away.

"Wait," they said.

I looked back.

"Does the meal cost anything?"

"No."

"Are you sure?"

"Yes. People contribute if they can. People eat if they're hungry."

They studied the bowl in their hands.

"Someone told me I could help wash dishes."

"You can. But you don't have to earn your food."

Their face tightened in a way I recognized. Sometimes people had been given so much conditional kindness that an uncomplicated offer felt like a trap.

"I don't want to be counted," they said.

"Then we won't count you."

I set the chair nearby, not close enough to imply they had accepted it. Then I walked back to the others.

When I returned later with fresh water, they were sitting in it.

Iroh noticed the change.

He came beside me as the first lanterns lit above us.

"You did not try to persuade them."

"They said no."

"And then they found their way to yes."

"Maybe. Or maybe they just wanted a chair."

He smiled.

"Both can be true."

Across the square, Greg was teaching Maui a chorus. Maui sang far too loudly. Katara laughed when Toph demanded a better rhythm. Danse and Tamsin had finally repaired the sixth table, and Mara was inspecting it with the suspicion of someone who had been betrayed by furniture before.

By the time the bread ran low, people had begun volunteering things the feast didn't need. A visiting merchant offered a brass serving bell in exchange for having his name announced. Maui considered giving a speech. Greg considered giving the bell a drum solo. Mara considered locking the pantry.

“Food first,” she said. “Then furniture. Then anybody who wants a solo can perform it outside.”

Greg held up both hands. “I was mostly kidding.”

“Mostly is doing a lot of work,” I told him.

Iroh caught my eye. “We may have a problem with the number of people asking for seconds.”

“Do we have enough?”

“We have enough for the children and the workers who haven't eaten yet. After that, no.”

He didn't make the shortage disappear. He asked Mara which portions she had reserved for volunteers, then checked the counts with her instead of inventing a more generous number. When a visitor complained, Iroh explained the limit in the same patient voice he'd used to greet him. There was an edge beneath the courtesy that reminded me of a commander holding a line.

Greg set the guitar aside to help carry water, and Maui was given the very unglamorous task of folding chairs. He tried to bow while holding three at once. Toph told him that if he dropped one, he would have to listen to her describe the sound for a week.

Danse inspected the fixed table with Tamsin and signed the repair sheet. Their signatures mattered more than the banner. Six places at a table weren't six invitations if somebody could lose their seat to a loose screw.

Mara's last basket went to the kitchen volunteers. A couple from the far district brought their own food and chose to eat near the open arch instead of joining the circle. No one chased them with an invitation.

I was glad the feast wasn't perfect. The ledger would have a real total, the music would end when people were tired, and we would all have to return the borrowed chairs. That felt like a celebration inhabited by people rather than a painting of one.

Iroh reached for my hand beneath the edge of the serving cloth.

"You have been running all day," he said.

"So have you."

"Perhaps we should set a poor example and rest."

"I could be convinced."

He poured the last two cups from the special pot. The tea was faintly sweet. I took mine and sat beside him on the steps, watching the celebration continue without us.

A gentle breeze lifted the hem of my sleeve. Iroh brushed a crumb from the edge of my mouth with his thumb, then waited.

"You have an audience," I murmured.

"Then they will have to practice looking elsewhere."

I leaned into his kiss. It was warm and soft and lasted long enough for the music to become background noise.

When we parted, I heard a small cough.

Mara stood behind us with a tray.

"If you two are finished being disgustingly sweet, somebody has to put the cups away."

Iroh accepted the tray with perfect dignity.

"I am told love involves service."

"Love can carry the dishes," Mara said.

So we did.

By the end of the evening, all six tables were occupied, nobody had been forced into a seat, and the quiet guest had gone home with a loaf of bread they hadn't needed to earn.

For a festival advertised with so much optimism, that seemed like a reasonable success.
